messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Clinical Vignette: Aroha

Aroha was twenty when her husband Marcus hit her for the first time. It happened in their apartment on a Thursday evening after she'd mentioned, casually, that she'd run into an old friend at the grocery store. The conversation escalated quickly—Marcus accused her of flirting, of betraying him, of being unfaithful in her heart if not in fact. When she tried to leave the room, he grabbed her arm and struck her across the face. The sound of his hand connecting with her cheek echoed in the small kitchen. What stayed with her most vividly was not the pain but the shock of his presence suddenly becoming dangerous, the way his body had moved toward her with an intention she'd never seen before. After that night, there were three more incidents over the next two months, each one preceded by his jealous accusations, each one followed by apologies and promises. Then Aroha found the courage to leave.

That was eight months ago. Now, at twenty-one, she works as an interior designer for a small firm in Auckland, but her life has contracted in ways she struggles to articulate. Loud noises—a car backfiring, a door slamming, even the sound of a male colleague's voice raised in conversation—send her into a state of acute alarm. Her body floods with adrenaline, her chest tightens, and she finds herself scanning the room for exits or places to hide. Being alone with any man, even her father, triggers an immediate sense of danger. When her supervisor, a kind man named David, approached her desk last week to review a design project, Aroha's hands began to shake so badly she could barely hold the colour swatches. The physical proximity, the maleness of his presence, the closed office door behind him—all of it conspired to make her certain, in that moment, that something terrible was about to happen. When he left, her heart continued racing for twenty minutes.

Aroha has come to believe that her life has been destroyed by what happened to her. She tells her therapist that she no longer belongs anywhere—not in her marriage, which she left; not in her workplace, where she feels exposed and unsafe; not even in her own apartment, where she now sleeps with every light on and checks the locks compulsively. The conviction that people cannot be trusted has calcified into something almost axiomatic. She watches colleagues interact and sees only potential betrayal. When her mother calls, Aroha hears the concern in her voice and interprets it as judgment. This sense that the world is fundamentally unsafe and that she is fundamentally alone has made her hypervigilant in ways that exhaust her. She finds herself constantly scanning faces, listening for threats in tone of voice, positioning herself so that she can always see the door. Her body never fully relaxes—even when she is sitting at her desk designing a client's living room, her muscles remain tense and ready to react, as if danger might emerge at any moment.

The memories themselves are fragmented and overwhelming. When she tries to explain to her therapist what happened that night, the words scatter. She can describe the kitchen, the colour of his shirt, the exact angle of his arm as he raised it, but the narrative collapses. She loses the thread of cause and effect, the sequence dissolves, and she is left feeling like she has failed to communicate something crucial. More often, the memory comes not as a coherent story but as a flood of pure emotion—terror, shame, a crushing sense of guilt—without any accompanying image. She wakes sometimes with her heart hammering and no memory of a dream, only the residual feeling that she has done something unforgivable. The guilt is particularly insidious. Aroha replays the evening obsessively, hunting for the moment where she could have prevented it. She should not have mentioned her friend. She should have noticed the tone in Marcus's voice earlier. She should have been more careful, more aware, more compliant. These thoughts loop endlessly, and each cycle deepens her conviction that she is to blame for what happened to her.

This self-blame drives her avoidance in ways that have begun to isolate her further. She has stopped going out after dark, which means she declines social invitations and makes excuses to colleagues. She avoids being alone in any room or building—she arrives at the office early when others are there and leaves before the last person departs. She turns down projects that would require her to work in clients' homes, citing scheduling conflicts. At night, she cannot tolerate darkness, so she keeps lights on throughout her apartment, which has made her electric bill astronomical and has deepened her sense of being trapped in a life that no longer makes sense. The avoidance feels necessary, protective, but it also feels like a slow suffocation. Each time she sidesteps a situation that reminds her of the event—the dark, being alone, the proximity of men—she reinforces her own conviction that these situations are genuinely dangerous, that her fear is justified, that the world outside her carefully controlled routines is a place where terrible things happen to women like her.

Last week, she saw Marcus at a shopping centre. He was across the mall, talking to someone near a shop window, and he did not see her. But she did see him. The recognition was instantaneous and total. Her vision narrowed, her breath became shallow, and within seconds she was in a state of panic so severe that she had to sit down on a bench and wait for her body to stop shaking. The encounter lasted perhaps thirty seconds, but it has reverberated through her week. She has not been able to sleep properly since. Loud noises now startle her even more acutely. Being in the office feels more dangerous. The memory of that evening has surfaced repeatedly, each time with the same fragmented quality and the same overwhelming guilt. She finds herself ruminating more intensely on her own culpability, and her conviction that she belongs nowhere has deepened into something close to despair.

Aroha came to her first therapy appointment because her mother finally insisted, saying she was worried her daughter was disappearing. Aroha herself is not certain what she hopes therapy will do. What she knows is that she is afraid—of loud sounds, of men, of being alone, of the memories that come unbidden and leave her paralyzed with shame. She is afraid that this is permanent, that she will never feel safe again, that the person she was before that Thursday evening is gone forever. She is hoping, though she barely dares to say it aloud, that someone might help her understand why she blames herself for being hit, why her own mind has become as dangerous as the man who hurt her, and whether there is any way back to a life that feels like it belongs to her.
